newsitem.title: USA: US jury finds Du Pont guilty but mentally ill.
newsitem.headline: US jury finds Du Pont guilty but mentally ill.

text.p: A Pennsylvania jury on Tuesday found millionaire chemicals heir John du Pont guilty of third degree murder but mentally ill in the killing of Olympic champion wrestler David Schultz.
The six man and six woman jury announced its verdict after deliberating since last Tuesday.
The verdict implies that du Pont killed Schultz with malice, but without the premeditation that would have been required for a first degree murder conviction.

The mental illness provision means du Pont will face the same penalty as an ordinary third degree murder verdict, but will be allowed to receive mental health treatment before serving out any remainder to his term.
The maximum penalty for the conviction is 20 to 40 years, but sentencing guidelines specify a sentence of 69 months to 10 years.

Du Pont also was found guilty but mentally ill on simple assault charges for pointing a gun at a security consultant who accompanied him to the killing, but was found innocent of the same charge for pointing a gun at Schultz's widow, Nancy.

Lawyers for du Pont, 58, had acknowledged he killed Schultz at the wrestler's home on the du Pont estate in January 1996, but argued du Pont suffered from paranoid schizophrenia that rendered him incapable of knowing right from wrong.

Testimony over the 13-day trial featured numerous instances of bizarre behaviour by du Pont, who was described as suffering delusions that he was the Dalai Lama, the last czar of Russia or the Christ child.

Incidents recalled by witnesses included his ordering portions of his estate dug up to search for the corpse of a chambermaid he imagined to be his actual mother, and du Pont's emergence from an armoured personnel carrier, martini cocktail in hand, to greet a visting policeman.
Prosecutors agreed du Pont was mentally ill, but said he knew killing Schultz was wrong, and acted out of anger and resentment over Schultz's popularity in the wrestling world.
Du Pont was a long-time fan and patron of amateur wrestling, and established training facility on his sprawling Foxcatcher Farm estate in suburban Philadelphia.
Schultz worked as a coach at the facility and lived with Nancy and their two young children in a house on the estate until the day he was shot.

According to eyewitness testimony during the 13-day trial, du Pont drove up to Schultz while the wrestler was working on a car in his driveway, then pumped three bullets from a .44 calibre handgun into Schultz before driving away. The third shot was fired into Schultz as he lay motionless face down in the snow.
The shooting was followed by a 48-hour police siege of du Pont's mansion before he was captured.
Du Pont is a great-great grandson of E.I. du Pont, who in 1802 founded the chemical company that bears his name and formed the basis of one of the largest family fortunes in the United States.
The personal wealth of John du Pont has been estimated at up to $250 million.
Du Pont might face additional legal action. Shortly after the killing, Mrs. Schultz retained lawyers for a possible civil suit.
She said earlier she would consider a suit after the criminal trial. "Right now, I just want to get him behind bars," she said.
